requests.discriminates: the five predicates are equality tests against the three named constants, so a byte outside the domain answers false to all of them, including the two OrUnknown predicates that a range check would have answered true
requests.subject: core.Tristate

requests.discriminates: only TSUnknown is replaced: a set value keeps its own value even when the default is unknown, an out-of-domain byte is returned unchanged rather than treated as unset, and an unknown default leaves the result unknown
requests.subject: core.Tristate

requests.discriminates: false converts to TSFalse (1), never to the zero value TSUnknown (0), so an option explicitly set to false stays distinguishable from an unset one
requests.subject: core.Tristate

requests.discriminates: the marshaller's default arm emits null for everything that is not TSTrue or TSFalse, so unknown and an out-of-domain byte are indistinguishable in the encoded form and the mapping is not round-trippable
requests.subject: core.TristateJson

requests.discriminates: UnmarshalJSON switches on the exact bytes it is handed and never reports an error, so a quoted, padded or malformed literal silently becomes TSUnknown; reaching it through encoding/json changes the answer, because the decoder strips the surrounding whitespace and rejects a syntax error before the method is ever called
requests.subject: core.TristateJson

requests.discriminates: the constructor takes int arguments and stores int32 fields, so a position beyond the int32 domain is truncated rather than clamped or rejected, and Pos/End report the truncated value: 2^31 reads back as the most negative position and 2^32 reads back as zero
requests.subject: core.TextRange

requests.discriminates: Len subtracts in int32 and only then widens, so a range spanning the whole int32 domain reports -1 and the reversed extreme range reports 1; a reversed ordinary range reports a negative length instead of zero
requests.subject: core.TextRange

requests.discriminates: IsValid ORs its two endpoint tests, so a range with one non-negative endpoint is valid while UndefinedTextRange is not; Contains is half-open, ContainsInclusive admits the end and ContainsExclusive admits neither bound; Intersects treats touching ranges as intersecting where Overlaps does not; and CompareTextRanges falls through to the ends only when the positions tie. The position argument and the comparison result are machine ints rather than the stored int32: a position of 2^32 stays outside the range instead of being folded to 0, WithPos truncates that same argument to 0 the way NewTextRange does, and CompareTextRanges widens both endpoints before subtracting, so the int32 extremes report -4294967295 and 4294967295 where an int32 subtraction would wrap to 1 and -1, which is the wrap Len does report
requests.subject: core.TextRangePredicates

requests.discriminates: the extension is everything after the last dot, lowercased with strings.ToLower and matched whole: a bare '.ts' is a TS file, 'a.d.ts' is plain TS, and the fold is ASCII-only in effect, because the only two non-ASCII runes that lower to ASCII produce 'i' and 'k', which appear in no recognized extension. The last two names pin that boundary: a dotted-capital-I suffix and an invalid UTF-8 byte must both stay Unknown rather than being folded or replacement-decoded into a match
requests.subject: core.ScriptKind

requests.discriminates: only Unknown is defaulted to TS, so a .json or .jsx file keeps its own kind while an unrecognized or extensionless name becomes TS and is never left at the zero value
requests.subject: core.ScriptKind

requests.discriminates: TS is not a case of the switch: it reaches .ts through the same default arm as Unknown, the two reserved values and any out-of-domain kind, so the extension cannot be used to recover the kind it came from
requests.subject: core.ScriptKind

requests.discriminates: a second star makes the parse return the zero Pattern, whose StarIndex is 0 and whose Text is empty, not the -1 that means an exact match; the parsed empty exact pattern has the same empty Text but keeps StarIndex -1 and is valid, so the recorded star index and IsValid each separate the two, and IsValid is the only predicate that rejects the zero value, because Matches panics on it instead of answering false
requests.subject: core.Pattern

requests.discriminates: prefix and suffix may overlap in the candidate: 'abab' matches 'ab*ab' with an empty captured text, and the shortest candidate a one-sided pattern accepts captures nothing without the end index running past the start. An exact pattern matches but captures the empty string rather than the whole candidate
requests.subject: core.Pattern

requests.discriminates: the star index, the prefix and suffix tests and the capture are all byte offsets, so a pattern and a candidate that are not valid UTF-8 are compared and captured verbatim; a decode-then-match implementation would collapse each invalid byte to U+FFFD and match candidates this one rejects
requests.subject: core.Pattern

requests.discriminates: Matches does not consult IsValid first: on the invalid zero Pattern the length guard passes, because len(Text)-1 is -1, and the suffix slice Text[1:] then runs off an empty string, so a caller that skipped IsValid panics instead of getting false. MatchedText panics separately when the candidate simply does not match. Only the panic class is compared, because the two runtimes word the same failure differently
requests.subject: core.Pattern

requests.discriminates: an exact match resets the longest prefix length to -1 rather than to its own length, so a later star pattern whose star index is 0 displaces it, while the same two patterns in the other order keep the exact match; among star patterns the longest literal prefix wins regardless of position, and when nothing matches the result is the zero value of the element type, which the 1-based indices here keep distinguishable from a real selection
requests.subject: core.Pattern

requests.discriminates: the rendering of a Tristate outside its three named values. The generated method guards with `i < 0 || idx >= len(_Tristate_index)-1` (tristate_stringer_generated.go:22), but Tristate is a byte (tristate.go:8), so the signed half of that guard is dead and the numeric fallback is reached only past the index table. A port that modelled Tristate as a three-variant enum could not render 3, 4 or 255 at all, and a port that modelled Tristate as a signed i8 renders 255 as Tristate(-1) where the pin renders Tristate(255). 255 is the largest value the byte can hold, so this trace also fixes where the fallback's numeric text ends.
requests.subject: core.Tristate

requests.discriminates: the hole at 5. ScriptKind is not densely numbered: the declared values run 0..4 and then jump to 6 (scriptkind_stringer_generated.go:11-16), so the generated method is a switch over two runs (:27-34) rather than one index lookup, and 5 renders as the numeric fallback while 6 renders as a name. A hand-written match that walked a table of the six declared values in order would hand 5 the name that belongs to 6 and shift every later value. This stringer also keeps the type prefix -- it is generated without -trimprefix, unlike ModuleKind and ScriptTarget -- so the names are ScriptKindTS rather than TS, which a port sharing one naming helper across the enums would get wrong. The i32 extremes fix the fallback's text at both ends of the domain.
requests.subject: core.ScriptKind

requests.discriminates: the two-value enum whose guard is live. LanguageVariant is an int32 (languagevariant.go:6), so unlike Tristate -- which shares this index-table shape -- the generated `i < 0` test at languagevariant_stringer_generated.go:21 can actually fire, and a negative value takes the numeric fallback rather than indexing the table backwards. The names keep the type prefix, so they are LanguageVariantStandard and LanguageVariantJSX rather than Standard and JSX. A port that rendered a bare JSX differs on the two named values; a port that clamped an out-of-domain value to Standard instead of reporting the number differs on the unnamed ones on five of these seven values.
requests.subject: core.LanguageVariant

requests.discriminates: the two numeric gaps between ModuleKind's three runs. The declared values are 0..7, 99..102 and 199..200 (modulekind_stringer_generated.go:11-24), so the generated method is a three-arm switch over three separate name strings (:39-51), each arm subtracting its own base before indexing. 8, 98, 103, 198 and 201 therefore render as ModuleKind(n), and this is exactly where a hand-written Rust match would differ: the port has two private renderings of this operation and they already disagree with each other -- crates/tsr_checker/src/emit_checks.rs:514 names all fourteen values, while crates/tsr_compiler/src/verify_options.rs:584 names only Node16..NodeNext and renders ModuleKind(1) where the pin renders CommonJS. The names are trimmed of the ModuleKind prefix, because this stringer is generated with -trimprefix and ScriptKind's is not.
requests.subject: core.ModuleKind

requests.discriminates: the gap between ES2025 and ESNext, and the two aliases that share a number. ScriptTarget declares 0..12 and 99..100, so the generated method is a two-arm switch (scripttarget_stringer_generated.go:40-49) and 13..98 render as ScriptTarget(n) -- the range a port that treated the enum as contiguous would fill with invented names. ScriptTargetLatest is 99 and ScriptTargetLatestStandard is 12 (scripttarget_stringer_generated.go:26-27), so those two numbers must render as ESNext and ES2025: a port that gave an alias its own name would differ there without being wrong about any declared value. The names are trimmed of the ScriptTarget prefix, and 100 is JSON rather than ScriptTargetJSON.
requests.subject: core.ScriptTarget
